title: Urban renewal and gentrification: who gains, who is displaced, and the policy responses

parts.label: A
parts.demand: Give the information asked for: a word or short phrase can earn the point, with no reasons needed.
parts.prompt: Identify one characteristic of a city neighborhood that often makes it attractive to gentrification.

rubric.point: Names a characteristic that draws higher-income newcomers or investors to a neighborhood.
accept: older, well-built housing that is cheap to buy
location close to downtown or to job centers
access to rail or bus transit
low property prices or rents compared with nearby areas
historic architecture or a waterfront

parts.sample: Older, well-built houses that sell for low prices close to downtown.

parts.label: B
parts.demand: Give the relevant characteristics: what it is like, where and how much. A name alone earns nothing.

rubric.point: Describes higher-income residents or investors moving into a lower-income neighborhood and raising property values, rents or the cost of living there.
accept: wealthier people buy and renovate homes in a poorer area, and prices and rents rise
investment flows into a low-income neighborhood, changing who lives there and what shops serve it

parts.sample: Higher-income residents and investors move into a lower-income neighborhood, buy and renovate older buildings, and open new shops, so property values, rents and taxes in the neighborhood rise and its population becomes wealthier.

parts.label: C
parts.demand: Say how or why, with every link of the chain: a cause, then because or so, then its effect, tied to the place or data asked about.
parts.prompt: Explain one way gentrification can benefit a city government.

rubric.point: Explains a benefit with its link, such as rising property values increasing property tax revenue, or new businesses adding jobs and sales tax.
accept: property values rise, so the city collects more property tax to pay for services
new businesses open, so the city gains jobs and sales tax revenue
renovation reduces abandoned buildings, so the city spends less on vacant properties

parts.sample: As newcomers renovate homes, property values rise, so the city collects more property tax, which it can spend on schools, parks and transit.

parts.label: D
parts.demand: Say how or why, with every link of the chain: a cause, then because or so, then its effect, tied to the place or data asked about.
parts.prompt: Explain how gentrification can lead to the displacement of long-time renters.

rubric.point: Explains that rents or property taxes rise faster than long-time residents' incomes, so they can no longer afford to stay and must move.
accept: rising demand pushes rents up faster than renters' wages, so they are priced out
landlords sell or renovate buildings and raise rents, so long-time tenants must leave

parts.sample: Demand from higher-income newcomers pushes rents up faster than long-time renters' wages rise, so many renters can no longer afford their homes and are forced to move to cheaper areas.

parts.label: E
parts.demand: Give a similarity or a difference and say it about both things, not one.
parts.prompt: Compare urban renewal and gentrification as causes of neighborhood change.

rubric.point: Gives a similarity or difference that speaks of both, such as urban renewal being led by government clearing and rebuilding, whereas gentrification is mostly driven by private buyers and investors; or both bring investment and can displace residents.
accept: urban renewal is government-led clearance, whereas gentrification is led by private buyers renovating
both bring new investment to a low-income area and both can displace long-time residents

parts.sample: Urban renewal is led by government, which buys, clears and rebuilds whole areas, whereas gentrification is usually driven by private buyers and investors renovating buildings one at a time; both bring investment and both can displace long-time residents.

parts.label: F
parts.demand: Say how or why, with every link of the chain: a cause, then because or so, then its effect, tied to the place or data asked about.
parts.prompt: Explain how one policy at the local scale can reduce the displacement of residents in a gentrifying neighborhood.

rubric.point: Names a local policy and explains how it keeps housing affordable for existing residents.
accept: inclusionary zoning requires a share of affordable units in new buildings, so some lower-income families can stay
a community land trust owns land and keeps homes at affordable prices, so residents are not priced out
rent help or limits on rent increases keep housing costs within reach, so renters can stay
property tax relief for long-time owners keeps their costs down, so they can stay

parts.sample: A city council can pass inclusionary zoning that requires new apartment buildings to set aside a share of units at prices lower-income families can pay, so some long-time residents can stay in the neighborhood as it changes.

parts.label: G
parts.demand: State the degree first (to a high, moderate or low degree), then explain why with evidence.
parts.prompt: Explain the degree to which push and pull factors explain why long-time residents leave a gentrifying neighborhood.

rubric.point: States a degree first (high, moderate or low), then explains it with at least one push or pull factor and why that factor does or does not fully explain the move.
accept: to a high degree: rising rent pushes residents out and cheaper housing elsewhere pulls them, though some are forced out by eviction
to a moderate degree: rising rent is a push factor, but many residents do not choose to move; eviction or demolition forces them, which is closer to forced migration

parts.sample: To a moderate degree. Rising rents and the loss of familiar shops act as push factors, and cheaper housing in the suburbs acts as a pull factor, so the model explains many moves. But many renters do not really choose to leave: when a building is sold or demolished they are evicted, so their move is closer to forced migration than to a free response to push and pull factors.
